text: Mr Hartigan came down the steps of the house in Eccles Street and stood a moment in the grey light, settling his hat. The morning was raw and the gulls cried over the rooftops towards the river. He had meant, for years now, to write to his brother in Cork, and each Sunday he told himself the letter would be written. He thought of the ink dried in the well on the parlour shelf, of the pen his wife had given him the Christmas before she died. A milk-cart went by, the horse blowing, and the boy on it touched his cap without looking. Hartigan returned the salute out of long habit. At the corner the newsboys were shouting some news of England, and he did not buy a paper. He stood with his gloved hands joined behind him and felt the cold creep up through the soles of his boots. There was nothing now to keep him in the city and nothing to take him out of it. The bells of George's Church began, far off and thin, and he counted them without meaning to. When they had finished he turned and went back up the steps and let himself in, and the hall was dark and smelled faintly of damp and of the dinner he would eat alone.

She had said she would meet him under the clock at Amiens Street and he was early, as he was always early. The trains came in with their long sighs of steam and the people poured past him with their parcels and their tired faces, and he watched the women, each one not her, until his watching became a kind of ache. He had bought her a brooch in a shop on Henry Street, a small thing of pressed tin made to look like silver, and it was warm now in his waistcoat pocket from the heat of his hand. A porter trundled a barrow of luggage close and he stepped back against the wall. He remembered how she had laughed at the Rotunda, her head tilted, and how he had thought then that a man might build a whole life on such a laugh. The clock above him moved with its small dry click. When the half hour struck and she had not come he told himself she had been kept by her mother, that the trams were slow. He waited until the lamps were lit and the platform emptied and a cleaner began sweeping the far end, and still he stood, the brooch growing cold against him, unwilling yet to give it the name it had.

The aunts kept the room warm for the card-players and the gas hissed gently in its mantle. Mrs Conroy dealt with a practised flick of her thin fingers and old Mr Devereux, who had been a clerk at Guinness's forty years, arranged his hand close to his chest as though someone might still rob him of it. The talk went round, as it always went, to the funerals of the season and the price of coal and the disgrace of young Lacey who had gone to America and never written. Nobody spoke of the war. From the next room came the sound of a girl at the piano picking out a melody she could not quite remember, breaking off, beginning again. Mr Devereux laid down a trump and won the trick and smiled at no one. He was thinking of a winter long ago when he had walked a girl home along the canal at Portobello and the swans had been black shapes upon the black water. He could not now recall her face, only the cold of it and the way the gaslight had lain in pools along the path. He gathered the cards. The girl in the next room found her tune at last and played it through, and for a moment the room was very still.

Every evening after the shop was shut Corley walked out the Drumcondra Road to where the houses thinned and the fields began, and he told himself it was for the air. He was a big soft man going to fat, and the assistants laughed at him behind the counter, he knew, though they were civil to his face. At the bridge he stopped and leaned on the parapet and looked at the dark water going under, and he thought about the money. There was a sum put by in the Munster and Leinster, more than anyone guessed, and he turned it over in his mind the way a man turns a smooth stone in his pocket. He had meant it once for a wife and a house with a garden. Now he could not say what he meant it for. A boy went past on a bicycle, whistling, and the lamp on it threw a small wavering light. Corley watched it dwindle and vanish round the turn. The fields beyond were a soft grey nothing and somewhere a dog barked twice and was quiet. He felt the chill of the stone come through his coat and he straightened himself and turned back towards the lamps of the town, and the whole way home he was careful not to think at all.

The retreat was over and the boys filed out of the chapel into the wet yard, subdued, their collars damp. Flynn walked with his head down, the priest's words still moving in him like cold water. He had meant to be good. He had meant it every year and every year the meaning wore thin by Easter, like the elbows of his jacket. Across the yard the lay brother was ringing the bell for tea and the rooks lifted off the elms in a black ragged cloud and settled again. Flynn thought of his mother in the parlour at home, the lamp turned low, waiting up for letters that said he was doing well. He thought of the half-crown he had taken from her purse and spent on toffee and the music-hall, and how he had told himself it was nothing. Now the nothing sat in his chest like a swallowed stone. He stood a moment apart from the others by the wall where the ivy hung black and dripping. A bigger boy called to him to come on out of the rain and he went, slipping a little on the wet flags, and the dull obedient line of them moved in under the arch, and the bell went on ringing in the grey air above the city.
